title: Ad click aggregation
summary: Streaming aggregation with event time, dedup and reconciliation.
prompt: Design a system that counts ad clicks per ad per minute for advertiser dashboards and billing. Counts must be near real time for dashboards and exact for invoices.

requirements: Functional: record clicks, aggregate per ad per minute (and other dimensions), query recent and historical counts, filter invalid clicks.
Non-functional: dashboards within a minute or two; billing counts exact and auditable; tolerate late and duplicate events.
estimation: Raw events ~200 bytes ⇒ 200 GB a day; aggregates (ads × minutes) are much smaller.
2M active ads × 1,440 minutes ≈ 2.9B potential rows a day, but most ad-minutes are empty, so store only non-zero ones.
api: Click redirect endpoint records {clickId, adId, userHash, timestamp, ip} then redirects to the advertiser.
data: Raw click log in a durable, partitioned stream and archived to object storage (source of truth for audits).
Aggregates: (ad_id, minute) → count in an OLAP or wide-column store; rolled up to hours and days.
design: Click service writes events to a partitioned stream (keyed by ad ID) and redirects immediately.
A stream processor deduplicates by click ID, filters invalid clicks, and aggregates into event-time tumbling windows of one minute, writing results to the aggregate store.
A daily batch job recomputes counts from the archived raw log; billing uses the batch result and reconciles it with the streaming totals.
deepDives: Event time vs processing time: windows use the click timestamp; watermarks decide when a window is complete; late events within an allowed lateness update the window, later ones go to the batch correction.
Exactly-once counts: checkpoint processor state together with stream offsets, and make sink writes idempotent (upsert by ad and minute) so replays do not double count.
Hot ads: pre-aggregate within each partition or add a random sub-key then combine.
bottlenecks: Bot and fraud traffic: rules and models filter clicks; invalid clicks are kept but flagged.
Backpressure when sinks slow: the stream buffers; scale processors by partitions.
Query load on dashboards: precomputed rollups and caching.
tradeoffs: Lambda-style (stream + batch) gives fast and exact results at the cost of two code paths; a single streaming path is simpler if it can be made exact.
Longer allowed lateness = more accurate streaming counts but later finalisation.
Keeping raw logs is expensive but essential for audits and recomputation.

rubric.text: Logged raw clicks durably before redirecting.
Aggregated in event-time windows with watermarks and late-event handling.
Deduplicated clicks and made sink writes idempotent.
Separated near-real-time dashboards from exact billing counts.
Kept raw data for recomputation and audits.
Estimated event rates and aggregate sizes.
Addressed click fraud and explained lambda vs kappa trade-offs.
